objectives: Define opportunity cost, then identify and calculate it for a set of alternatives.
Identify sunk costs and analyze decisions with marginal thinking by comparing marginal benefit and marginal cost.
Use the production possibilities frontier to explain a society's choices, efficiency, and increasing opportunity cost.

concepts.definition: The value of the best alternative given up when you make a choice. It includes not only money you pay but also the value of time, income, or experiences you give up.
The limit on the combinations you can buy, set by the money (or time) you have and the prices you face. Buying more of one good means giving up the other good in proportion to their price ratio.
A cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered no matter what you choose. A rational decision about the future leaves it out.
Deciding by comparing the marginal benefit of doing a little more with its marginal cost. If the marginal benefit is greater than the marginal cost, do more; if it is smaller, stop.

A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced with given resources and technology. Points on the curve are efficient, points inside it are inefficient, and points outside it are currently unattainable.

As production of one good keeps rising, resources less suited to that good must be shifted into it, so the amount of the other good given up for each additional unit grows. This is why the production possibilities frontier bows outward.

beginner.summary: When you choose something, the real cost is the most valuable thing you gave up. Forget the money you have already spent, and weigh the gains and losses of doing a little more.

sections.heading: The real cost is what you give up
paragraphs: Suppose you could earn $30 at a part-time job on Saturday afternoon for 3 hours, but you go to the movies with a friend instead. Is the ticket price your only cost? No. You also gave up the $30 you could have earned. The most valuable thing you give up because of a choice is called its opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Choosing within your budget
paragraphs: When your spending money is fixed, so are the combinations you can buy. Hypothetically, if a matinee movie ticket costs $8 and a slice of pizza costs $4, seeing one more movie means giving up two slices of pizza. Prices tell you what you give up, and how much.

sections.heading: Forget the money you already spent
paragraphs: You bought a non-refundable concert ticket, and on the day of the show you feel sick. It's easy to think, "I paid for it, so I have to go." But you won't get the ticket money back whether you go or not. A cost that is already spent and can't be recovered is called a sunk cost. For your decision, compare only what you would gain and lose by going from now on.

sections.heading: A little more, or stop here?
paragraphs: The night before a test, when you're deciding whether to study one more hour, don't focus on how many hours you've already studied. Instead, compare how much one more hour would help with how much you'd lose by sleeping less. Weighing the benefit and cost of a little more is called marginal thinking.

sections.heading: Choices for a whole country
paragraphs: A country also has a limited number of workers, amount of land, and number of machines, so growing more rice means making less clothing. At first, the land best suited to farming is used, so giving up a little clothing adds a lot of rice. But as rice production keeps growing, workers and land better suited to factory work have to be moved into farming, and much more clothing must be given up. The curve connecting all these possible combinations is the production possibilities frontier.

intermediate.summary: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone. Rational decisions ignore sunk costs and compare marginal benefit with marginal cost. The production possibilities frontier shows opportunity cost for society as a whole.

sections.heading: Opportunity cost
paragraphs: Opportunity cost = explicit costs (money actually paid) + implicit costs (the value of income and time given up). The cost of going to college includes not only tuition but also the income you would have earned by working during those years. Note that opportunity cost is not the sum of all the alternatives given up but only the single most valuable one, because you could not have done all of them at the same time.

sections.heading: Budget constraints and price ratios
paragraphs: The budget line shows the limit on the combinations you can buy with a budget m at the prices of two goods. To buy one more unit of one good, you must give up the other good in an amount equal to the ratio of the two prices. Hypothetically, if a movie ticket costs $8 and a pizza slice costs $4, the opportunity cost of one movie is two pizza slices.

sections.heading: Sunk costs and marginal thinking
paragraphs: A sunk cost has already been spent and cannot be recovered; it is the same whichever option you choose, so it should not affect your decision. A rational decision compares the marginal benefit (MB) and marginal cost (MC) of one more unit: keep increasing the activity while MB ≥ MC, and stop once MB < MC. For many activities, marginal benefit declines as you do more, so there is a natural point to stop.

In reality, people do not always act rationally; they may cling to sunk costs or choose out of habit. The rationality assumption in economics is a simplified starting point for understanding behavior.

sections.heading: The production possibilities frontier
paragraphs: Points on the production possibilities frontier are combinations that use all resources efficiently. Points inside the curve involve unemployment or waste, and points outside it cannot be reached with current resources and technology. Moving along the curve, the amount of one good given up to produce more of the other is the opportunity cost. Because resources differ in how well suited they are to each use, this opportunity cost rises, so the curve bows outward. Technological progress or more resources shift the entire curve outward.

advanced.summary: Rational choice means maximizing net benefit subject to constraints, which requires marginal benefit = marginal cost. The slope of the production possibilities frontier is the marginal opportunity cost, and efficiency comes in two forms: productive efficiency and allocative efficiency.

sections.heading: Formalizing opportunity cost and the budget constraint
paragraphs: From the budget constraint p₁x₁ + p₂x₂ = m, we get x₂ = m/p₂ − (p₁/p₂)x₁, so the slope of the budget line is −p₁/p₂. The absolute value of the slope, p₁/p₂, is the opportunity cost of one unit of good 1 measured in units of good 2. An increase in income shifts the budget line outward in parallel, while a change in one good's price changes its slope.

sections.heading: Maximizing net benefit and sunk costs
paragraphs: Let B(q) be the total benefit and C(q) the total cost of an activity level q. At the q that maximizes net benefit B(q) − C(q), marginal benefit equals marginal cost (in discrete terms, you continue up to the last unit for which MB ≥ MC). A sunk cost F is the constant term in C(q) = F + V(q); it does not affect MC and therefore does not change the optimal q. Reasoning that "we have already invested so much that we must continue" is the sunk cost fallacy.

sections.heading: The production possibilities frontier and efficiency
paragraphs: At any point on the production possibilities frontier, the absolute value of the slope is the marginal opportunity cost of producing one more unit of a good. Every point on the curve satisfies productive efficiency (maximum output with no waste), but only the combination society most prefers satisfies allocative efficiency. So "Is it efficient?" and "Is it desirable?" are different questions, and which point to choose depends on society's preferences and value judgments.

worked_examples.title: The opportunity cost of a Saturday afternoon
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: On Saturday afternoon you have 3 hours, and you can do only one of these: (1) work a part-time job that pays $10 per hour, (2) see a movie with a friend, or (3) relax at home. You choose the movie, and you think the job is worth more than relaxing. How much money did you give up by seeing the movie?
steps: The most valuable alternative you gave up is the part-time job.
Money you could have earned at the job: $10 × 3 = $30.
worked_examples.answer: $30 (plus the price of the movie ticket). Relaxing is worth less to you than the job, so it is not added to the opportunity cost.

worked_examples.title: Opportunity cost as a price ratio
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: You have $24 a month for entertainment, which you spend on movie tickets ($8 each) and pizza slices ($4 each). What is the opportunity cost of one movie in pizza slices? If you see two movies, what is the maximum number of pizza slices you can buy?
worked_examples.answer: The opportunity cost of one movie is 2 pizza slices. If you see two movies, you can buy at most 2 pizza slices.

worked_examples.title: How many hours to study: marginal benefit and marginal cost
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: A student is deciding how long to study the night before an exam. The marginal benefit of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th hours (the value of the grade improvement, expressed in dollars) is $12, $9, $6, and $3, respectively. Each hour of study gives up $6 worth of other activities (rest or sleep). How many hours of study is rational, and what is the net benefit?
steps: Hour 3: $6 = $6 → studying causes no loss. Hour 4: $3 < $6 → don't study.
With 3 hours of study, total benefit = $12 + $9 + $6 = $27 and total cost = $6 × 3 = $18.
Net benefit = $27 − $18 = $9 (the same $9 as with 2 hours).
worked_examples.answer: Studying 2 or 3 hours is rational, with a net benefit of $9. In the 4th hour, the marginal benefit is smaller than the marginal cost, so it would reduce net benefit.

worked_examples.title: The production possibilities frontier and increasing opportunity cost
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: An island community can produce the following combinations of (rice in tons, cloth in bolts) per year: (0, 100), (10, 90), (20, 70), (30, 40), (40, 0). How many bolts of cloth are given up when rice production rises from 20 to 30 tons, and how does the opportunity cost change along the curve?
steps: Rice 0→10: cloth 100→90, so 10 bolts given up. 10→20: 20 bolts. 20→30: 70 − 40 = 30 bolts. 30→40: 40 bolts.
For each additional 10 tons of rice, the cloth given up grows: 10, 20, 30, 40 bolts.
worked_examples.answer: 30 bolts of cloth are given up. The opportunity cost of rice rises as more rice is produced (increasing opportunity cost), so the curve bows outward.

real_world_examples.title: The real cost of more education
paragraphs: When weighing the cost of college or job training, you should count not only spending such as tuition and textbooks but also the income you would have earned by working during that time. This forgone income can make up a large share of the opportunity cost.

real_world_examples.title: Society's choices and the production possibilities frontier
paragraphs: How a society divides its resources among health care, education, national defense, environmental protection, and other goals can also be seen as a choice of a point on a production possibilities frontier. Expanding one area means cutting another, and deciding which combination is desirable takes more than efficiency; it requires society's value judgments.

sdg_case.title: Single-use dishes at a school fair: weighing the opportunity costs
paragraphs: SDG target 12.5 calls for substantially reducing waste generation through prevention, reduction, recycling, and reuse.

Hypothetical scenario: Your class has a fixed budget and limited time to prepare a food booth for the school fair. You need to decide what dishes to serve the food in. Compare the opportunity cost (money, time, and effort) of each option along with how much waste it would prevent.

options.name: Use single-use plates and cups
benefits: Setup and cleanup take the least time, so that time can go to selling and promotion.
costs: It creates a lot of waste.
New plates and cups have to be bought every time.
assumptions: The class does not directly pay for waste disposal or the environmental burden.

options.name: Borrow reusable dishes and wash them yourselves
benefits: Spending on dishes may go down.
costs: Washing takes people and time, which can't be used for other preparation (an opportunity cost).
assumptions: A place to wash and enough water are available, and hygiene standards can be met.

options.name: Give a discount to customers who bring their own cup or container
benefits: Waste goes down while the class has little washing to do.
costs: Revenue falls by the amount of the discount.
Customers who don't bring a container still need dishes.
assumptions: The discount is large enough that customers actually bring their own containers.

discussion: Write down the opportunity cost of each option in time and money. Comparing those costs with how much waste each option prevents, what combination of options would work best?

key_takeaways: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up, including both money paid and the value of income and time forgone.
Ignore sunk costs when deciding about the future, and decide whether to do a little more by comparing marginal benefit and marginal cost.
The production possibilities frontier shows a society's choices and opportunity costs, and it bows outward because of increasing opportunity cost.
